key_insight: Multi-agent collaboration is not always better: for capable language models, adding more agents can eventually stop helping and even hurt performance. The paper shows this tipping point can be predicted well enough to choose the best setup in most cases.
problem_solved: It addresses the practical question of when to use single-agent vs. multi-agent LLM systems, since collaboration can improve reasoning in some settings but introduce overhead, redundancy, or conflict in others.
method: Evaluated large language model agents across 260 controlled system configurations.
Measured how performance changes with different collaboration architectures, agent counts, and task conditions.
Trained a predictive model to recommend the best architecture and tested it on held-out within-domain configurations.
impact: This helps AI practitioners avoid assuming that more agents automatically means better results. It provides a data-driven way to design LLM systems that balance accuracy, efficiency, and complexity.
visual_elements: A side-by-side diagram comparing single-agent and multi-agent workflows.
A line chart showing performance gains and eventual saturation/decline as collaboration scales up.
A decision tree or selector graphic for choosing the best architecture based on task conditions.
A heatmap of the 260 configurations highlighting where collaboration helps vs. hurts.
paper_title: Capable language models can outgrow the benefits of collaboration
paper_authors: Yubin Kim, Ken Gu, Chanwoo Park, Chunjong Park, Samuel Schmidgall
